name: Gareth Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the customer line for a parcel delivery firm, calls and chats. Mostly it's where's my parcel, and the rest is lost or damaged claims. I use AI all day, it pulls up the tracking and drafts the claim notes, and I've built a few shortcuts of my own that the team now uses. What wears me out is having to say sorry for drivers I've never met.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm twenty-seven and live with Rosa, my girlfriend, she cuts hair in a salon in town. I've got about nine months of pay saved and a shares account I add to every month. Sundays I take my nan to Mass and then we all have lunch at my mum's. My brother Luis runs a man-and-van removals business, and I do his bookings and website on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the market decided. If AI doesn't pay for itself, firms won't buy it, and that's how it should be. I'd probably post something like that, I'm the one in the group chat who argues about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a bit disappointing, because I like the tools. But my job's safe and I'd keep using the bits that work. Not much changes for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using my shortcuts and keep adding to the shares account, about two-fifty a month. I'd do more on Luis's removals business, maybe set up online quotes so he gets more jobs. And I'd go for a supervisor role at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said disappointing. What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feeling of being ahead. Right now I'm the guy who knows the AI tools at the parcel firm, and being ahead is worth something. If AI fizzles, that edge goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything weighing on you right now, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Rosa wants to rent her own salon chair, which costs money up front. We've got enough, so it's more planning than worry.

I'd argue it out in the **group chat**, as I always do.
think: It'd be a bit **disappointing**, because I like the tools.
My job's **safe**, and I'd keep using what works.
do: Keep adding about **£250 a month** to my shares account.
Set up **online quotes** for Luis's removals business.
Go for a **supervisor role** at the depot.

fieldNote: Gareth's **edge** at work comes from knowing the AI tools best.

steps.text: Keep adding 250 a month to the shares account

Apply for a supervisor role at the parcel depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and the people who learn will be fine. I'd tell my team to start using the tools now, not wait. I'd not be sympathetic to anyone who refuses outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, where's my parcel calls are the first thing to go. A bot can read tracking as well as me. I'd want to be the person who runs the bot, not the person it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to set up the new bot at work, in the first month. I'd push Luis to grow the removals business, because people moving house still need strong arms. And I'd keep investing, maybe in the delivery firms themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not be sympathetic to people who refuse. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit hard. My nan would tell me off for that. But I think people have to help themselves first, then family helps, and only after that does anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Rosa talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to put money into Luis's business, maybe buy a second van. Rosa would want to see the numbers first. She's more careful than me.

think: **Where's my parcel** calls go first, because a bot reads tracking well.

Push Luis to **grow the removals** business.
S1.quote: People have to help themselves first, then family helps, and only after that does anyone else.
fieldNote: Gareth's **free-market** view is softened by his nan's influence.
He'd move **first** to run the new bot.
He sees **removals** as hands-on work that lasts.

steps.text: Volunteer to set up the parcel firm's new chatbot
Put savings into a second van for Luis's removals business
Grow Luis's removals bookings through a new website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and we need to stop pretending it isn't. I'd say people should move fast, not wait for government help. I'd probably post a long thread about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the customer line is gone within a year. Even running the bot probably goes, because AGI runs itself. The removals business with Luis is hands-on, so it has about three years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the parcel firm in the first year and join Luis full time. We'd buy a second van, run it with AI for bookings and routes, and grow fast while the robots aren't here yet. I'd also keep investing, because the companies making this will be worth a fortune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots come for removals, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for removals would come around 2031, so my brother Luis and I would grow fast, then sell the business to someone who wants the customers. I'd have made what I can in three years and hopefully own some shares that went up. I'd be honest that I don't know after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your nan about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be fine, and I'd look after her. She'd say pray about it. I probably would, actually.

say: I'd say this is **huge** and people should move fast.
I'd say don't wait for **government help**, in a long online thread.
think: The customer line is **gone within a year**, even running the bot.
Removals with Luis has about **three years longer**.
do: Leave the parcel firm and join Luis's **removals business** full time.
Buy a **second van** and use AI for bookings and routes.
S2.quote: Robots for removals would come around 2031, so my brother Luis and I would grow fast, then sell the business to someone who wants the customers.
fieldNote: Gareth sees the **robot gap** as a business window, not a refuge.
His plan is to **build and sell** before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, and people should start now. I'd talk about it at Sunday lunch and probably annoy everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is enough to build the removals business properly. I'd keep the parcel job for a year or two while it grows. Then I'd jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and put weekends into Luis's business, then go full time in year two. We'd add a second van and maybe a third. I'd use AI for everything on the office side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd stop the holidays abroad for a couple of years and put the money into vans. Rosa would want her salon chair too, so we'd balance it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager Steve is fifty and hates computers. He's a good man, but he won't change. I'd try to get him a job at my brother's removals firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great chance and people should take it. I'd say government should stay out of the way and let people get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. Ten years is enough to build the business and sell it before the robots. I'd be thirty-seven with money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the parcel firm a few years, go for supervisor, and build the removals business on the side. Then go full time around year three or four. Rosa and I would buy a house and maybe start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A family changes things. Would you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My nan always says there's never a perfect time to start a family. With ten years of warning, we'd have time to set up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me getting greedy, maybe. Buying too many vans too fast. Rosa would keep me in check.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because everything happens at once and even a good plan could fail. What would help is lower taxes on small businesses, so people like Luis and me can grow fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much this depends on family. I've got Luis, my mum, my nan and Rosa. A lot of people at the parcel firm don't have family like mine to lean on, and they'll have it much harder.

headlineQuote: A lot of people at the parcel firm don't have family like mine to lean on, and they'll have it much harder.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** parcel firm customer agent who uses AI tools every day.
He lives with Rosa, a hairdresser, and has **nine months saved** plus a shares account.
He's **free-market** and traditional, close to his nan and brother Luis.
He stays calm or uneasy except under **fast AGI**, where he turns anxious.
His plan is to grow Luis's **removals business** and sell it before robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because everything happens at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** on small businesses so they can grow fast.
